rows.source: HSE workplace exposure limits
rows.verified: Employers must protect workers from hazardous dusts, fumes, chemicals, vapours, mists, gases, nanomaterials and biological agents.

rows.source: HSE workplace exposure limits
rows.verified: For carcinogens, mutagens and asthmagens, COSHH requires exposure to be controlled as low as reasonably practicable.

rows.source: HSE workplace exposure limits
rows.verified: Exposure can occur by inhalation, skin contact, injection through the skin or swallowing.

rows.source: HSE workplace exposure limits
rows.verified: Workplace exposure limits are approved GB occupational limits for concentrations of hazardous substances in air averaged over defined periods.

rows.source: HSE workplace exposure limits
rows.verified: Only a subset of substances used at work have workplace exposure limits.

rows.source: HSE workplace exposure limits
rows.verified: EH40 lists current Great Britain workplace exposure limits for use with COSHH.

rows.source: HSE workplace exposure limits
rows.verified: Workplace exposure limits are only one part of the control measures required under COSHH.

rows.source: HSE workplace exposure limits
rows.verified: Where older guidance conflicts with revised limits, the current EH40 table takes precedence.

rows.source: HSE workplace exposure limits
rows.verified: WEL interpretation depends on substance identity, sampling method, averaging period, exposure route, mixtures, task pattern and control reliability.

rows.source: HSE workplace exposure limits
rows.verified: An air limit does not by itself determine individual dose, health outcome or an exact parcel-level probability.

rows.source: HSE hairdressing COSHH and dermatitis controls
rows.verified: Frequent contact with water and shampoo can irritate skin and contribute to dermatitis.

rows.source: HSE hairdressing COSHH and dermatitis controls
rows.verified: Hairdressing and cleaning products can cause dermatitis and allergic skin reactions.

rows.source: HSE hairdressing COSHH and dermatitis controls
rows.verified: Dusty products such as persulphates and henna can cause occupational asthma.

rows.source: HSE hairdressing COSHH and dermatitis controls
rows.verified: Some hair sprays can aggravate asthma symptoms.

rows.source: HSE hairdressing COSHH and dermatitis controls
rows.verified: Workplaces should maintain suitable ventilation to reduce airborne exposure.

rows.source: HSE hairdressing COSHH and dermatitis controls
rows.verified: Smooth disposable non-latex gloves are advised for relevant wet and chemical tasks.

rows.source: HSE hairdressing COSHH and dermatitis controls
rows.verified: Hands should be dried thoroughly, moisturised and checked regularly for early skin changes.

rows.source: HSE hairdressing COSHH and dermatitis controls
rows.verified: Gloves should be changed between clients to avoid prolonged contamination and cross-contact.

rows.source: HSE hairdressing COSHH and dermatitis controls
rows.verified: Hairdressing risk depends on product chemistry, wet-work duration, ventilation, glove selection, aerosol generation, task and individual sensitisation.

rows.source: HSE hairdressing COSHH and dermatitis controls
rows.verified: Hairdressing evidence is product-, task-, exposure-, client- and worker-specific and is not an exact parcel-level asthma or dermatitis probability.
